title: Signature Family Council
body:
The Signature Family Council is an original design for household decisions: a council that meets weekly, with a rotating chair, a visible agenda, and a decision book. The chair rotates among household members old enough to hold it, including teenagers, so chairing is a shared skill rather than an adult privilege. The agenda is posted the day before, anyone may add an item, and decisions are written in the book with the date and the person responsible. The council's rule is that every decision is reviewed at the next meeting, so a bad decision is corrected quickly instead of becoming a permanent grievance.

Method. The working method for this record is a council routine. First, post the agenda the day before the meeting. Second, rotate the chair each week. Third, work through items in agenda order, giving each speaker an uninterrupted turn. Fourth, write each decision in the book with a responsible person and a review date. Fifth, open the next meeting by reviewing last week's decisions before adding new items.

Use and limits. Use this design as a household organization tool. Keep meetings short and regular rather than long and rare.

title: Signature Check-in Wheel
body:
The Signature Check-in Wheel is an original design for weekly check-ins: a wheel divided into sections for each household member, spun to choose who speaks first, so the same person does not always open. Each section holds three prompts: one good thing, one hard thing, and one need for next week. The wheel's point is fairness of order and sameness of questions: everyone answers the same three prompts, including adults, so check-ins do not become interrogations of children by adults. The wheel is a physical or drawn object, deliberately simple, because a check-in tool that needs charging or logging in will be skipped.

Method. The working method for this record is a wheel routine. First, draw or make the wheel with one section per member. Second, spin to choose the first speaker each week. Third, each member answers the three prompts in turn. Fourth, the listener repeats back what was heard before offering advice. Fifth, the family picks at most one practical change for the coming week and writes it down.

title: Signature Listening Chair
body:
The Signature Listening Chair is an original design for listening without fixing: a designated chair, or a designated cushion, where the rule is that the person sitting in it speaks and the person standing listens without offering solutions until asked. The chair makes the listening rule physical and visible, which helps children understand it: when someone sits in the listening chair, the household knows a story is being told and advice is on hold. The listener's only jobs are attention, reflection, and the question of whether the speaker wants ideas, comfort, or time alone.

Method. The working method for this record is a chair routine. First, choose the chair and agree its rule together. Second, when someone sits in it, the listener stops other tasks and gives full attention. Third, the speaker finishes without interruption. Fourth, the listener reflects the feeling and the facts and checks the summary. Fifth, the listener asks what the speaker wants: ideas, comfort, or time alone, and honors the answer.

title: Signature Repair Letter Kit
body:
The Signature Repair Letter Kit is an original design for apologizing in writing when a spoken apology is too hard or too heated: a kit with a template and four blanks. Blank one names what happened. Blank two names the writer's own part. Blank three states the apology in specific words. Blank four proposes one change for next time. The letter is given without demanding a reply, and the recipient may answer in writing or in person when ready. Written repair helps where spoken repair derails, because a letter can be drafted, cooled, and corrected before it is given.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-blank letter. First, write what happened in neutral words. Second, write the writer's own contribution honestly. Third, write a specific apology for that contribution. Fourth, propose one change for next time. Fifth, give the letter without demanding an immediate reply, and accept a written or spoken answer when the recipient is ready.

title: Signature Screen Dial
body:
The Signature Screen Dial is an original design for household screen agreements: a dial per child, and one for the household, with four positions for leisure screens. Position zero is a screen-free day. Position one is a short day. Position two is a standard day. Position three is a long day, such as a weekend or holiday. The dial is set the evening before, so the day's screen plan is known before the day begins, and changing the dial mid-day requires a family discussion rather than a unilateral decision. Homework and creative screens sit outside the dial, because they are task-based rather than time-based.

Method. The working method for this record is a dial set nightly. First, agree the dial's four time values for school days and weekends separately. Second, set each dial the evening before. Third, treat homework and creative screens as task-based and outside the dial. Fourth, change a dial mid-day only by agreement. Fifth, review the dial's values monthly, because children's needs change and a dial that never moves becomes ignored.

title: Signature Toddler Screen Gate
body:
The Signature Toddler Screen Gate is an original design for toddler screen routines: a gate with three questions that must all be answered yes before a screen is switched on. Is it short and calm. Is an adult watching together. Is it outside meals and the time before sleep. If any answer is no, the gate stays closed and the toddler's activity is play, stories, or outdoor time instead. The gate is deliberately strict and simple, because toddler routines fail when they depend on judging each program's quality in the moment.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-question gate. First, check short and calm. Second, check together viewing with an adult who talks about the program. Third, check that the time is not a meal or pre-sleep time. Fourth, if the gate opens, watch together and talk about what is on screen. Fifth, notice mood and sleep after screen days and adjust the routine if either worsens, closing the gate more often if needed.

title: Signature School Screen Plan

Homework screens happen at a desk in a shared room. Creative screens happen where making is possible. Social screens happen at agreed times. Entertainment screens happen in shared rooms and never in the hour before bed. title: Signature Teen Screen Contract
body:

The contract is signed by everyone and reviewed monthly, with the teenager proposing changes with reasons, so the contract grows with maturity instead of being outgrown and ignored.

title: Signature Game Night Charter
body:

How long is a session. How does a session end: clock time or natural break. On which days and at which times. Who may be played with and how voice chat works. What spending is allowed. Method. The working method for this record is a five-line charter. First, agree session length and the ending rule. Second, agree allowed days and times. title: Signature Readiness Ladder
body:
The Signature Readiness Ladder is an original design for social media readiness: a ladder with rungs that a young person climbs before an account is created. Rung one is understanding that posts can be copied and kept. Rung two is setting an account to its most private setting. Rung three is practicing reporting and blocking. Rung four is agreeing household rules for posts and for unkind messages. Rung five is a trial period with a review date. The ladder's point is that readiness is demonstrated rung by rung, not granted by reaching a birthday, and a young person who climbs the ladder with a parent learns the safety tools before problems arise.

Method. The working method for this record is a rung-by-rung climb. First, work through each rung together, with the young person doing the settings themselves. Second, check each rung by demonstration, not by promise: the privacy setting is shown, the reporting tool is practiced. Third, agree the trial period and its review date. Fourth, review the trial together and adjust the rules. Fifth, keep climbing: new platforms mean new ladders, because settings and risks differ by platform.

title: Signature Homework Screen Splitter
body:
The Signature Homework Screen Splitter is an original design for separating homework screens from leisure screens on the same device: a splitter with two sides, task side and leisure side, each with its own rules. The task side is time-open but task-closed: it ends when the task ends, and it happens in a shared room where help is available. The leisure side is time-closed: it ends at an agreed time, wherever it happens. The splitter can be physical, such as different profiles or app timers, or procedural, such as homework first followed by leisure, but it must be visible, because a split that exists only in memory will be forgotten under pressure.

Third, set the leisure side's rule: agreed time, agreed place. Fourth, make the split visible with profiles, timers, or a posted plan. title: Signature Family Calendar Board
body:
The Signature Family Calendar Board is an original design for household organization: a board, physical or shared digital, with two halves, calendar and chores. The calendar half shows everyone's commitments for the week in one place, so clashes are seen early. The chores half lists recurring tasks, who does each one, and when it rotates, so work does not fall silently on one person. Children help choose their chores, and completed work is marked visibly, because a board that only tracks failures teaches children to avoid it.

Method. The working method for this record is a weekly board routine. First, gather everyone's commitments into the calendar half. Second, list recurring chores, assign them, and rotate the less popular ones. Third, post the board where everyone sees it. Fourth, hold a short weekly review to move tasks and resolve clashes. title: Signature Distance Bridge
body:
The Signature Distance Bridge is an original design for long-distance family contact: a bridge with three spans. The first span is a regular call at a predictable time. The second span is a light midweek touch, such as a photo or short message. The third span is longer contact on a calendar everyone sees, such as visits or long calls. The bridge's rule is predictability: a grandparent who calls every Sunday is part of the week, while unpredictable calls are pleasant surprises that cannot be counted on. Children get a role on the bridge, such as choosing a story to read over video or a question to ask, so contact is theirs as well as adults'.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-span rhythm. First, choose the regular call time, fitting time zones and routines. Second, add the midweek touch. Third, plan longer contact on a shared calendar. Fourth, give children a role in the contact. Fifth, review the rhythm when routines change, such as a new school term, rather than letting it fade silently.

title: Signature Two-Household Notebook

title: Signature Sibling Peace Table
body:
The Signature Sibling Peace Table is an original design for mediating sibling disputes at home: a small table, or a marked place, where the mediation rule applies. At the peace table, each child speaks without interruption, the parent reflects each side's wants in neutral words, the children brainstorm solutions together, and they choose one to try. The table's rule is that the parent is a helper, not a judge, and that the children own the chosen solution, so they learn to reuse the skill when no adult is present. If the same dispute returns, the table's second rule applies: look for the underlying cause, such as a shared space or a scarce item, and change the household arrangement rather than mediating the same argument again.

Method. The working method for this record is a table routine in five steps. First, calm the situation, separating children briefly if needed. Second, let each child speak without interruption. Third, reflect each side's wants neutrally. Fourth, brainstorm solutions together without judging ideas. Fifth, let the children choose a solution and check later whether it worked.
